accepted.question_text: Let G be a 3-connected cubic graph with a blue-red vertex coloring. Write B and R for the subgraphs induced by the blue and red vertices. A crumby coloring is one with maximum degree Delta(B) <= 1, minimum degree delta(R) >= 1, and no path with 3 edges in R. Since the original conjecture asserting that every 3-connected cubic graph has such a coloring is false, what relaxation of the conditions imposed on the red induced subgraph R is sufficient to guarantee that every 3-connected cubic graph admits a blue-red coloring of this type?

evidence.quote: Consider a blue-red vertex coloring of a 3-connected cubic graph G. Denote by B and R the subgraphs of G induced on blue and red vertices, respectively. In [2] Thomassen conjectured that there is always such a blue-red coloring of G where Delta(B) <= 1, delta(R) >= 1 and R does not contain a path with 3 edges. Such a coloring is known as a crumby coloring.

However, the conjecture on crumby colorings is false. Hence, the following question arises: Problem 1.1 What relaxation of the conditions on R guarantees that such a coloring of a 3-connected cubic graph always exists?

accepted.question_text: For a graph G, let chi_l(G) be the least integer k such that every k-list-assignment L admits a proper L-coloring, and let chi*_l(G) be the least integer k such that for every k-list-assignment L, the graph G admits an L-packing of size k, meaning k pairwise-disjoint L-colorings. Does there exist a graph G for which the list packing number exceeds the list-chromatic number by at least 2, that is, chi*_l(G) > chi_l(G) + 1?

evidence.quote: The list-chromatic number (or choosability) chi_l(G) of a graph is the minimum integer k such that every k-list-assignment L admits an L-colouring. Given a k-list-assignment L of G we call a collection of k pairwise-disjoint L-colourings an L-packing of size k, or less specifically a list-packing. The list packing number chi*_l(G) of G is the least k such that G admits an L-packing of size k for any k-list-assignment L of G.
Problem 2.1 Is there a graph G for which chi*_l(G) > chi_l(G) + 1?

accepted.question_text: For every graph G, is the list packing number chi*_l(G) always at most twice the list-chromatic number chi_l(G)? Equivalently, if chi_l(G) is the least k such that every k-list-assignment admits a proper coloring and chi*_l(G) is the least k such that every k-list-assignment admits k pairwise-disjoint proper colorings, must chi*_l(G) <= 2 chi_l(G) hold for all graphs G?

evidence.quote: The list-chromatic number (or choosability) chi_l(G) of a graph is the minimum integer k such that every k-list-assignment L admits an L-colouring. Given a k-list-assignment L of G we call a collection of k pairwise-disjoint L-colourings an L-packing of size k, or less specifically a list-packing. The list packing number chi*_l(G) of G is the least k such that G admits an L-packing of size k for any k-list-assignment L of G.
Problem 2.2 Is it true that chi*_l(G) <= 2chi_l(G) for every graph G?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a cubic planar graph and let L be a 3-list-assignment on G, meaning each vertex has a list of three allowed colors. An L-coloring is proper if adjacent vertices receive different colors, and two L-colorings are disjoint if every vertex receives different colors in the two colorings. Must every such 3-list-assignment admit two disjoint proper L-colorings?

evidence.quote: An L-colouring of G is a colouring c: V (G) -> N such that for every vertex v, c(v) in L(v). It is proper if adjacent u, v satisfy c(u) != c(v). Two L-colourings ci, cj are disjoint if ci(u) != cj(u) for every u in V (G).
For a 3-list-assignemnt of a cubic planar graph, we have the following problems: Problem 2.3 Is it possible to choose two disjoint proper colourings?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a cubic planar graph and let L be a 3-list-assignment on G. Is it always possible to choose three pairwise-disjoint proper L-colorings, that is, three proper colorings from the given vertex lists such that each vertex receives three different colors across the three colorings?

evidence.quote: An L-colouring of G is a colouring c: V (G) -> N such that for every vertex v, c(v) in L(v). It is proper if adjacent u, v satisfy c(u) != c(v). Two L-colourings ci, cj are disjoint if ci(u) != cj(u) for every u in V (G).
For a 3-list-assignemnt of a cubic planar graph, we have the following problems: Problem 2.4 Is it possible to choose three disjoint proper colourings?

accepted.question_text: For cubic bipartite graphs equipped with a 3-list-assignment, two disjoint proper colorings are known to exist. Does every cubic bipartite graph with a 3-list-assignment also admit three pairwise-disjoint proper list-colorings?

evidence.quote: In the case of cubic bipartite graphs, it is possible to find two disjoint proper colourings (problem similar to Problem 3) [unpublished]. Hence, the following question arises: Is it possible to find three disjoint proper colourings in the case of cubic bipartite graphs?

accepted.question_text: Fix an integer k >= 1 and let n = 4k + 1. Choose a set S subseteq {1, 2, ..., 2k} of size k, let the complementary set {1, ..., 2k} \ S be used on the second layer, and define the extended Petersen graph XP(2n, S) on vertex set Z_n x {1, 2} with layer edges determined by circular distance d(x, y) = min{|x - y|, n - |x - y|} and matching edges x1x2 for x in Z_n. Is every extended Petersen graph, except the Petersen graph itself, Class 1, meaning that its chromatic index equals its maximum degree?

evidence.quote: Let n = 4k + 1 for some integer k >= 1, and let S subseteq {1, 2, . . . , 2k} such that |S| = k. The extended Petersen graph XP(2n, S) is a graph with the vertex set V = Z_n x {1, 2}, and the edge set E = {x1y1 : d(x1, y1) in S} union {x2y2 : d(x2, y2) in S-bar} union {x1x2 : x in Z_n}, where S-bar = {1, . . . , 2k} \ S and d(x, y) = min{|x - y|, n - |x - y|}.
Conjecture 3.1 (Horak, Rosa [1]) Every extended Petersen graph, except Petersen graph itself, is of Class 1.
A graph G is Class 1 if it is Delta(G)-edge-colorable, otherwise it is Class 2.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a constant c >= 0 such that every non-complete graph G of order n with minimum degree delta(G) >= n/2 + c has rainbow connection number rc(G) = 2? In particular, does the weaker threshold delta(G) >= n/2 already imply rc(G) = 2?

evidence.quote: The minimum number of colors required so that the colored graph is rainbow connected, is called the rainbow connection number, and it is denoted by rc(G).
Problem 4.1 Does there exist a constant c >= 0 such that if G is a non-complete graph of order n with delta(G) >= n/2 + c, then rc(G) = 2? In particular, does delta(G) >= n/2 imply that rc(G) = 2?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a 5-edge-connected 5-regular graph that is Class 2, that is, a 5-regular graph whose edges cannot be colored with only 5 colors?

evidence.quote: A graph G is Class 1 if it is Delta(G)-edge-colorable, otherwise it is Class 2.
Surprisingly, it seems that no 5-edge-connected 5-regular Class 2 graph is known. Problem 5.1 (Ma, Mattiolo, Steffen, Wolf [1]) Is there any 5-edge-connected 5-regular Class 2 graph?

accepted.question_text: An r-graph is an r-regular graph G such that every odd vertex set X subseteq V(G) is joined to its complement by at least r edges. Such a graph is poorly matchable if any two of its perfect matchings intersect. Is there a poorly matchable 5-edge-connected 5-graph?

evidence.quote: An r-graph is an r-regular graph G such that every odd set X subseteq V (G) is connected by at least r edges to its complement V (G) \ X. An r-graph is poorly matchable if any two of its perfect matchings intersect.
Problem 5.2 Is there a poorly matchable 5-edge-connected 5-graph?

accepted.question_text: Can one characterize exactly which subcubic K3-free graphs are Class 2? Equivalently, is it possible to describe all K3-free graphs of maximum degree at most 3 whose chromatic index is 4 rather than their maximum degree?

evidence.quote: It is known that subdividing a single edge of a 3-edge colorable cubic graph yields an overfull subcubic graph G. Hence, G is of Class 2, i.e., chi'(G) = 4. Starting with a K3-free cubic graph, we produce, in that way, a K3-free subcubic graph of Class 2.
This raises the following question: Problem 6.1 Is it possible to describe all subcubic K3-free graphs of Class 2?

accepted.question_text: Let v1, ..., vn be a linear ordering of the vertices of a graph G, and for each vertex vi define d-(vi) = |{j < i : vivj in E(G)}| and d+(vi) = |{j > i : vivj in E(G)}|. A Type-A order is one in which every vertex v satisfies that d-(v) is odd or 0. Can it be decided in polynomial time whether a graph G admits a Type-A order or a Type-B order, where a Type-B order requires that each vertex either has d-(v) odd or 0, or else has d-(v) even and d+(v) = 0?

evidence.quote: Suppose that the vertices of a graph G are put in a linear order v1, . . . , vn. For i = 1, . . . , n define d-(vi) = |{j < i: vivj in E(G)}| and d+(vi) = |{j > i: vivj in E(G)}|.
Type-A order: for each v in V (G), d-(v) is odd or equal to 0; Type-B order: for each v in V (G), d-(v) is odd or equal to 0 (as in a Type-A order), or d-(v) is even and d+(v) = 0.
Problem 7.1 Can it be decided in polynomial time whether a graph G admits a Type-A order, or a Type-B order?

accepted.question_text: Under the same definitions of Type-A and Type-B vertex orders for a graph G, if G admits a Type-A order or a Type-B order, can such an order be found in polynomial time?

evidence.quote: Type-A order: for each v in V (G), d-(v) is odd or equal to 0; Type-B order: for each v in V (G), d-(v) is odd or equal to 0 (as in a Type-A order), or d-(v) is even and d+(v) = 0.
Problem 7.2 If a Type-A or Type-B order exists, can it be found in polynomial time?
